the same integral from t = 0⁻; equal to the bilateral one for causal signals; used with initial conditions
the values of s where the integral converges; a vertical strip that never contains a pole

key_terms.term: ROC of right-, left-, two-sided signals
key_terms.meaning: right of the rightmost pole; left of the leftmost pole; a strip between poles
X(jω) = X(s) at s = jω when the ROC contains the jω axis
e<sup>s₀t</sup>x(t) ↔ X(s − s₀); ROC moves by Re(s₀)
dx/dt ↔ sX(s) − x(0⁻); d²x/dt² ↔ s²X(s) − s x(0⁻) − x′(0⁻)
x₁(t) * x₂(t) ↔ X₁(s)X₂(s); ROC contains R₁ ∩ R₂
x(0⁺) = lim sX(s), s → ∞ (X strictly proper); x(∞) = lim sX(s), s → 0 (poles of sX(s) in the left half-plane)
Aₖ = [(s + pₖ)X(s)] at s = −pₖ for a simple pole
(s + a)ʳ needs r terms; 1/(s + a)ⁿ ↔ tⁿ⁻¹e⁻ᵃᵗu(t)/(n − 1)! when right-sided
H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) = L{h(t)} at initial rest
causal: ROC right of the rightmost pole; stable: ROC contains the jω axis; both: all poles in the left half-plane
zero-input response (initial conditions) + zero-state response (Y = HX)

takeaways: The Laplace transform weights x(t) by e<sup>−σt</sup> before the Fourier integral, so it exists for growing signals too, inside its region of convergence.
X(s) without its ROC is not an answer: 1/(s + a) is e<sup>−at</sup>u(t) for Re(s) > −a and −e<sup>−at</sup>u(−t) for Re(s) < −a.
The ROC is a vertical strip that never contains a pole: right of the rightmost pole for right-sided signals, left of the leftmost for left-sided ones, between poles for two-sided ones.
The properties build transforms from a few table pairs; the one-sided derivative rule brings the initial conditions into the algebra.
The final value theorem only works when every pole of sX(s) is in the left half-plane; check the poles before using it.
Partial fractions split a proper rational X(s) into table terms; repeated poles need every power, complex poles are kept as damped cosines and sines.
For an LTI system Y(s) = H(s)X(s); causal means the ROC is to the right of the rightmost pole, stable means the ROC contains the jω axis.
A pole on the jω axis is marginal, not stable: a step into 1/s gives a ramp, and an input at ω₀ into 1/(s² + ω₀²) grows without bound.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the ROC of a two-sided signal, the inverse transform for a stated ROC, and the stability and response of an LTI system from its transfer function. Long answers start from the defining integral or the factored H(s), state the ROC at every step, and close with a numerical check such as x(0⁺), x(∞) or X(0).

bank.q: Define the bilateral and one-sided Laplace transforms. Find X(s) and the ROC of x₁(t) = e<sup>−at</sup>u(t) and x₂(t) = −e<sup>−at</sup>u(−t), explain why the same X(s) describes two signals, and state the properties of the ROC.
outline: Both definitions with their limits, s = σ + jω
x₁: 1/(s + a), ROC Re(s) > −a, from the upper limit
x₂: 1/(s + a), ROC Re(s) < −a, from the lower limit
The ROC is part of the transform; it decides the side of the signal
ROC properties: strip, no poles, finite duration, right-, left- and two-sided cases
answer: Definitions. The bilateral Laplace transform is X(s) = ∫−∞∞x(t)e−stdt, and the one-sided transform is X(s) = ∫0⁻∞x(t)e−stdt. Here s = σ + jω is the complex frequency: σ = Re(s) in s⁻¹ and ω = Im(s) in rad/s. For a causal signal the two give the same result; the one-sided form is used when a system starts at t = 0 with initial conditions.

Meaning of σ. Since e−st = e−σte−jωt, X(s) is the Fourier transform of x(t)e−σt. Convergence depends on |x(t)|e−σt, that is on σ alone. The set of s where the integral converges is the region of convergence (ROC).

answer.text: Right-sided exponential x₁(t) = e−atu(t). Only t ≥ 0 contributes:
answer.pre:
X₁(s) = ∫ e⁻⁽ˢ⁺ᵃ⁾ᵗ dt   (t from 0 to ∞)
      = [ −e⁻⁽ˢ⁺ᵃ⁾ᵗ/(s + a) ] from 0 to ∞
      = 0 − ( −1/(s + a) ) = 1/(s + a)

answer: The value at the upper limit is 0 only if e<sup>−(s+a)t</sup> → 0 as t → ∞, which needs Re(s + a) > 0. So the ROC of x₁ is Re(s) > −a, the half-plane to the right of the pole s = −a.

answer.pre:
X₂(s) = −∫ e⁻⁽ˢ⁺ᵃ⁾ᵗ dt   (t from −∞ to 0)
      = −[ −e⁻⁽ˢ⁺ᵃ⁾ᵗ/(s + a) ] from −∞ to 0
      = −( −1/(s + a) − 0 ) = 1/(s + a)

answer: The value at the lower limit is 0 only if e<sup>−(s+a)t</sup> → 0 as t → −∞, which needs Re(s + a) < 0. So the ROC of x₂ is Re(s) < −a, the half-plane to the left of the pole.

Why one X(s) fits two signals. The algebra is the same, 1/(s + a), but the two integrals converge in different, non-overlapping half-planes. The pair (X(s), ROC) is what is unique: given the ROC, the inverse transform is fixed. So every transform must be written with its ROC.

head: Property
Statement
rows: a vertical strip σ₁ < Re(s) < σ₂ (σ₁ may be −∞, σ₂ may be +∞), because convergence depends only on σ
the ROC contains no pole; for rational X(s) it is bounded by poles or extends to infinity
an absolutely integrable signal of finite duration has the whole s-plane as ROC
ROC is Re(s) > σ₁, to the right of the rightmost pole
ROC is Re(s) < σ₂, to the left of the leftmost pole
ROC is a strip between two poles, or empty (then no transform exists)
X(jω) exists and equals X(s) at s = jω exactly when the ROC contains the jω axis

answer: Sketch for the answer sheet. Draw two s-planes with σ across and jω up. Mark the pole × at σ = −a on each. Shade everything to the right of the dashed line σ = −a for x₁, and everything to the left for x₂. For a > 0 the jω axis lies in the shaded part only for x₁. Examiners give a mark for this sketch, so draw it even when it is not asked for.

A finite-duration example. The pulse u(t) − u(t − 2) has X(s) = (1 − e−2s)/s. Near s = 0, e−2s ≈ 1 − 2s, so X(s) ≈ 2, which is finite: there is no pole at s = 0, and the ROC is the whole s-plane, as property 3 says.
Check. s = 0 lies in the ROC of x₁ for a = 2, so X₁(0) must equal ∫x₁(t)dt. X₁(0) = 1/2 and ∫₀∞e−2tdt = 1/2. They agree.

bank.q: State the time-shift and time-differentiation properties of the one-sided Laplace transform. Derive the differentiation property from the defining integral, extend it to the second derivative, and check both properties with a simple signal.
outline: Time shift: x(t − t₀)u(t − t₀) ↔ e<sup>−st₀</sup>X(s), t₀ > 0, ROC unchanged
Derivative: dx/dt ↔ sX(s) − x(0⁻), by integration by parts
Second derivative: s²X(s) − s x(0⁻) − x′(0⁻)
answer: Time shift. If x(t)u(t) ↔ X(s), then for a delay t₀ > 0, x(t − t₀)u(t − t₀) ↔ e−st₀X(s). Proof: put τ = t − t₀ in ∫t₀∞x(t − t₀)e−stdt to get e−st₀∫₀∞x(τ)e−sτdτ. The factor e−st₀ has no poles, so the ROC is unchanged.

answer.text: Derivative. Integrate by parts with u = e−st and dv = x′(t)dt:
answer.pre:
L{dx/dt} = ∫ x′(t)e⁻ˢᵗ dt                  (t from 0⁻ to ∞)
         = [x(t)e⁻ˢᵗ] from 0⁻ to ∞ + s∫ x(t)e⁻ˢᵗ dt
         = (0 − x(0⁻)) + s X(s)
         = s X(s) − x(0⁻)

answer: The upper-limit term vanishes for s inside the ROC, because x(t)e<sup>−st</sup> → 0 there. The lower-limit term leaves the initial value x(0⁻). The ROC of the result contains the ROC of X(s).

answer.text: Second derivative. Apply the rule to g(t) = dx/dt, whose transform is G(s) = sX(s) − x(0⁻):

answer: Why t₀ > 0. The one-sided integral sees only t ≥ 0⁻. With an advance (t₀ < 0), part of the shifted signal moves into t < 0 and is lost, so the rule no longer holds. In the bilateral transform x(t − t₀) ↔ e−st₀X(s) for any real t₀.

Why the rule matters. It turns a differential equation into algebra with the initial value built in. For y′ + 2y = 0 with y(0⁻) = 3: sY − 3 + 2Y = 0, so Y(s) = 3/(s + 2) and y(t) = 3e−2t for t ≥ 0, which starts at 3 as it should.

answer.text: Check of the derivative rule. Take x(t) = e−2t with x(0⁻) = 1, for example a capacitor voltage that was already 1 V before t = 0.

answer: Check of the time shift. u(t) ↔ 1/s. Delay by 3 s: the rule gives e−3s/s. Directly, ∫₃∞e−stdt = e−3s/s for Re(s) > 0. Both checks agree.

bank.q: State the initial value and final value theorems with their conditions. Use both on X(s) = 1/(s(s + 2)) and confirm by inversion, then give one case where the final value theorem gives a wrong answer.
outline: x(0⁺) = lim sX(s) as s → ∞, X strictly proper
x(∞) = lim sX(s) as s → 0, poles of sX(s) in the left half-plane
Failure: 4/(s² + 16) gives 0 but sin(4t) does not settle
answer: Initial value theorem. x(0⁺) = lim sX(s) as s → ∞. It holds when X(s) is strictly proper (numerator degree less than denominator degree), so that x(t) has no impulse at t = 0.

Final value theorem. x(∞) = lim sX(s) as s → 0. It holds only when the limit of x(t) exists, which is guaranteed when every pole of sX(s) lies strictly in the left half-plane. A simple pole of X(s) at s = 0 is allowed, because the factor s cancels it.
Initial value of X(s) = 1/(s(s + 2)). X is strictly proper (degree 0 over degree 2). sX(s) = 1/(s + 2) → 0 as s → ∞, so x(0⁺) = 0.
Final value. sX(s) = 1/(s + 2) has its only pole at −2, in the left half-plane, so the theorem applies: x(∞) = 1/(0 + 2) = 1/2.

answer.text: Confirm by inversion. Cover-up: A = 1/(0 + 2) = 1/2 at s = 0, and B = 1/(−2) = −1/2 at s = −2. So x(t) = ½(1 − e−2t)u(t).

answer: The table starts at 0 and settles at 0.5, as both theorems said.

A wrong answer. Take X(s) = 4/(s² + 16), the transform of sin(4t)u(t). Then sX(s) = 4s/(s² + 16) → 0 as s → 0, so a careless use says x(∞) = 0. But sin(4t) keeps swinging between −1 and +1 and has no final value. The theorem fails because sX(s) has poles at ±j4 on the jω axis, not in the left half-plane.

A wrong use of the initial value theorem. For the improper X(s) = (s + 2)/(s + 1) = 1 + 1/(s + 1), sX(s) → ∞ as s → ∞. The constant 1 is an impulse δ(t) at t = 0. Split it off first: the proper part 1/(s + 1) gives x(0⁺) = 1, which matches e−tu(t) at t = 0⁺.
Why the theorems work. As s → ∞, e−st shrinks to a narrow spike near t = 0, so sX(s) samples the start of x(t). As s → 0, e−st → 1 and sX(s) becomes the limit of x(t), when that limit exists.
Check. For 1/(s(s + 2)) the inverse at t = 1 s is ½(1 − e−2) = ½(1 − 0.135) = 0.432, between the initial value 0 and the final value 0.5.

bank.q: Define the transfer function, poles, zeros and BIBO stability of a continuous-time LTI system. State the pole condition for a causal system, apply it to H(s) = (s + 3)/(s² + 3s + 2), and explain why the integrator H(s) = 1/s is not BIBO stable.
outline: H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) = L{h(t)} at initial rest
Zeros: roots of N(s); poles: roots of D(s)
BIBO: every bounded input gives a bounded output; ∫|h(t)|dt finite; ROC contains the jω axis
Causal: stable exactly when all poles have Re < 0
1/s: h(t) = u(t), ∫|h| infinite; a step gives a ramp
answer: Transfer function. For an LTI system at initial rest, H(s) = Y(s)/X(s), the ratio of the transforms of output and input. Because y(t) = x(t) * h(t), the convolution property gives H(s) = L{h(t)}, the transform of the impulse response.
Poles and zeros. Write H(s) = N(s)/D(s). Zeros are the roots of N(s) = 0, where H(s) = 0. Poles are the roots of D(s) = 0, where H(s) is infinite. Each pole p gives a mode ept in h(t).

BIBO stability. A system is bounded-input bounded-output stable if every bounded input gives a bounded output. For an LTI system this holds exactly when ∫|h(t)|dt is finite, which in the s-domain means the ROC of H(s) contains the jω axis.

Pole condition. A causal system has its ROC to the right of the rightmost pole. That half-plane contains the jω axis exactly when the rightmost pole has a negative real part. So a causal rational system is BIBO stable if and only if every pole satisfies Re(p) < 0.

The integrator. H(s) = 1/s has a pole at s = 0, on the jω axis. Its impulse response is h(t) = u(t): bounded, but ∫₀∞|u(t)|dt is infinite. The causal ROC Re(s) > 0 does not contain the jω axis. A bounded input shows the failure: the unit step gives Y(s) = 1/s², so y(t) = t u(t), a ramp that grows without bound. The integrator is marginally stable, not BIBO stable.

Another marginal case. H(s) = 1/(s² + 4) has simple poles at ±j2, so h(t) = ½sin(2t)u(t) never decays. A bounded input at the same frequency, cos(2t)u(t), gives an output that grows like t sin(2t). So poles on the jω axis always fail the BIBO test, even though the impulse response itself is bounded.
Check. For the example, H(0) = 3/2, and ∫₀∞h(t)dt = 2·1 − 1·(1/2) = 3/2, as it must be when the ROC contains s = 0.

bank.q: Find the Laplace transform and the ROC of x(t) = e<sup>−3t</sup>u(t) − e<sup>−2t</sup>u(−t). Does the Fourier transform of x(t) exist?
outline: No Fourier transform: the strip misses the jω axis
answer: The second term is nonzero for t < 0, so use the bilateral transform and treat the two terms separately.
First term. e−3tu(t) ↔ 1/(s + 3), from ∫₀∞e−(s+3)tdt, with ROC Re(s) > −3.

answer.text: Second term. −e−2tu(−t) is the standard left-sided pair with a = 2:
answer.pre:
−∫ e⁻⁽ˢ⁺²⁾ᵗ dt  (t from −∞ to 0)  =  −[ −e⁻⁽ˢ⁺²⁾ᵗ/(s + 2) ] from −∞ to 0
                                 =  1/(s + 2),   needs Re(s + 2) < 0

answer: So −e<sup>−2t</sup>u(−t) ↔ +1/(s + 2) with ROC Re(s) < −2. A common slip is to carry the minus sign of the signal into the transform and write −1/(s + 2); the minus sign is already used up by the left-sided integral.

ROC. Both conditions must hold: Re(s) > −3 and Re(s) < −2. The ROC is the strip −3 < Re(s) < −2, which is not empty, so the transform exists. It lies between the two poles, as a two-sided signal's ROC must.
Fourier transform. The strip does not contain σ = 0, so the Fourier transform does not exist. Indeed the left-sided part −e−2tu(−t) grows like e2|t| as t → −∞.

answer.text: Check at a point inside the ROC, s = −2.8.

answer: Invert back as a check. With the strip −3 < Re(s) < −2, the pole −3 lies to the left of the ROC, so 1/(s + 3) gives the right-sided e−3tu(t). The pole −2 lies to the right of the ROC, so 1/(s + 2) gives the left-sided −e−2tu(−t). Together they rebuild x(t) exactly.
Sketch. On the s-plane, mark × at −3 and at −2 and shade the narrow strip between them; the jω axis lies outside it, to the right.
Both forms give 3.75, so the combination is right. X(s) also has a zero at s = −2.5, inside the strip.

bank.q: Find the inverse Laplace transform of X(s) = (s + 2)/((s + 1)(s + 3)) for each possible ROC: Re(s) > −1, −3 < Re(s) < −1 and Re(s) < −3. Say which inverse has a Fourier transform, and check your answers.
outline: Only the first ROC contains the jω axis
answer: Proper? The numerator has degree 1 and the denominator degree 2, so no division is needed.
Poles. s = −1 and s = −3. They cut the s-plane into three possible ROCs: Re(s) > −1, −3 < Re(s) < −1 and Re(s) < −3.
Check the split. ½(s + 3) + ½(s + 1) = s + 2, the numerator. ✓
Rule for each term. If the ROC lies to the right of a term's pole −a, then 1/(s + a) ↔ e−atu(t). If it lies to the left, 1/(s + a) ↔ −e−atu(−t).

Fourier transform. Only the ROC Re(s) > −1 contains the jω axis (σ = 0). So only the right-sided inverse has a Fourier transform: X(jω) = (jω + 2)/((jω + 1)(jω + 3)). The other two contain e−tu(−t) or e−3tu(−t) terms, which grow as t → −∞.

Reading each case. In (a) both modes decay as t grows, so the signal is causal and dies out. In (b) the e−t term sits on t < 0 with a minus sign and grows towards t → −∞, while the e−3t term sits on t ≥ 0; the signal is two-sided. In (c) both terms sit on t < 0 and grow as t → −∞, so the signal is anti-causal.
Fourier transform of the right-sided answer at ω = 1 rad/s. X(j1) = (2 + j)/((1 + j)(3 + j)) = (2 + j)/(2 + 4j). So |X(j1)| = √5/√20 = 0.5.

Common slips. Writing u(t) for every term whatever the ROC; giving the strip answer as ½(e−t + e−3t)u(t); and putting the minus sign on the wrong term in case (b). Ask of each term: is the ROC to the right or to the left of this pole?
Check 1, initial value. For the right-sided answer, x(0⁺) = ½(1 + 1) = 1, and lim sX(s) = lim (s² + 2s)/(s² + 4s + 3) = 1 as s → ∞. ✓
Check 2, area. s = 0 is in the first ROC, so X(0) = ∫x(t)dt. X(0) = 2/(1·3) = 2/3. The area is ½(1 + 1/3) = ½ · 4/3 = 2/3. ✓

Check 3, the strip answer. Transform −½e−tu(−t) + ½e−3tu(t) back: the first term gives ½·1/(s + 1) for Re(s) < −1 and the second ½·1/(s + 3) for Re(s) > −3. The overlap is −3 < Re(s) < −1 and the sum is X(s). ✓
Conclusion. The algebra (A = B = 1/2) is the same for all three ROCs; the ROC alone decides the side of each term.

bank.q: Find the inverse Laplace transform of X(s) = 1/(s(s + 2)²) for the ROC Re(s) > 0.
outline: Checks: x(0⁺) = 0, x(∞) = 1/4, a test point
answer: Plan. Check that X(s) is proper, factor the denominator, write one term for every power of every repeated factor, find the coefficients (cover-up for the simple pole and the top power, the derivative rule for the lower power), then invert term by term using the ROC.
Form. X(s) is proper (degree 0 over 3). The pole at −2 is repeated twice, so X(s) = A/s + B/(s + 2) + C/(s + 2)².
Inverse. The ROC Re(s) > 0 is to the right of every pole, so every term is right-sided: 1/s ↔ u(t), 1/(s + 2) ↔ e−2tu(t), 1/(s + 2)² ↔ t e−2tu(t). Hence x(t) = (¼ − ¼e−2t − ½t e−2t)u(t).

answer.text: Same coefficients by comparing powers of s. Clear the denominator: 1 = A(s + 2)² + Bs(s + 2) + Cs.

answer: Common slips. Leaving out the B/(s + 2) term (then no choice of A and C fits the numerator), and taking B = +1/4 by losing the minus sign of d(1/s)/ds = −1/s².
Check 2, initial value. x(0⁺) = ¼ − ¼ − 0 = 0; the initial value theorem gives lim sX = lim 1/(s + 2)² = 0 as s → ∞. ✓
Check 3, final value. x(∞) = ¼ because both exponential terms decay; sX(s) = 1/(s + 2)² has its poles at −2, so the final value theorem applies and gives 1/4. ✓

bank.q: Solve dy/dt + 3y(t) = 2u(t) with y(0⁻) = 1 using the one-sided Laplace transform. Separate the zero-input and zero-state responses.
answer: Transform each term. L{dy/dt} = sY(s) − y(0⁻) = sY(s) − 1; L{3y} = 3Y(s); L{2u(t)} = 2/s.
Inverse. y(t) = 2/3 + (1/3)e−3t for t ≥ 0.

Meaning. The output starts at its stored value 1 and relaxes towards the forced value 2/3. The zero-input part is the stored energy leaking away; the zero-state part is the input charging the system from rest. An RC circuit whose capacitor holds 1 V and is driven towards 2/3 V behaves exactly like this.

Classical method as a cross-check. The homogeneous solution of y′ + 3y = 0 is Ke−3t, and a constant particular solution yp must satisfy 3yp = 2, so yp = 2/3. Then y(0) = K + 2/3 = 1 gives K = 1/3: the same y(t) = 2/3 + (1/3)e−3t. The Laplace route did the same work in one pass, with the initial condition already inside Y(s).

Check in the equation. y′ = −e−3t, so y′ + 3y = −e−3t + 2 + e−3t = 2 for t > 0. ✓ At t = 0, y = 2/3 + 1/3 = 1 = y(0⁻), as expected (no impulse in the input, so y does not jump). As t → ∞, y → 2/3, which is the steady value 2/3 from setting y′ = 0 in y′ + 3y = 2.

bank.q: A causal LTI system has H(s) = (s + 1)/(s² + 3s + 2). Find its poles and zeros, its impulse response and its unit-step response. Verify the step response by the convolution integral, and tabulate it for t = 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 s.
outline: Table of values; final value 1/2 = H(0)
answer: Factor. D(s) = s² + 3s + 2 = (s + 1)(s + 2). So H(s) = (s + 1)/((s + 1)(s + 2)): a zero at s = −1 and poles at s = −1 and s = −2.

Cancellation. The zero at −1 cancels the pole at −1, leaving H(s) = 1/(s + 2) for s ≠ −1. The cancelled pole is in the left half-plane, so no hidden growing mode is lost; the system is causal with ROC Re(s) > −2 and stable, because its remaining pole −2 has a negative real part.
Impulse response. h(t) = L⁻¹{1/(s + 2)} = e−2tu(t). The time constant is 1/2 s.

answer.pre:
y(t) = ∫ h(τ) x(t − τ) dτ = ∫ e⁻²ᵀ dτ   (τ from 0 to t)
     = [ −½ e⁻²ᵀ ] from 0 to t
     = ½(1 − e⁻²ᵗ)

answer: The convolution integral and the convolution property Y = HX give the same answer, as they must.

Without cancelling first. Y(s) = (s + 1)/(s(s + 1)(s + 2)). Cover-up on all three poles gives 1/2 at s = 0, 0/(−1·1) = 0 at s = −1, and (−1)/((−2)(−1)) = −1/2 at s = −2. The coefficient of the e−t mode is 0: the same answer.
Initial value of h(t). h(0⁺) = 1, and the initial value theorem gives lim sH(s) = lim s/(s + 2) = 1 as s → ∞. ✓
Initial value of the step response. sY(s) = 1/(s + 2) → 0 as s → ∞, so y(0⁺) = 0: the output starts from rest, as the table shows.

Frequency response. The ROC contains the jω axis, so H(jω) = 1/(jω + 2). At ω = 2 rad/s, H(j2) = 1/(2 + j2): gain 1/√8 ≈ 0.354 and phase −45°. So this system is a first-order low-pass filter with corner frequency 2 rad/s.

If the cancelled pole were unstable. Had the common factor been (s − 1), the reduced H(s) would still look stable from input to output, but the circuit would hold a hidden mode et that any initial charge sets growing. Here the cancelled factor is (s + 1), a decaying mode, so the cancellation is harmless.
Time constant and settling. The only mode is e−2t, so the time constant is 0.5 s and the step response is within 2% of 1/2 after about 4 time constants, 2 s (the table shows 0.491 at t = 2 s).

head: Item
Result
rows: zero −1; poles −1, −2; after cancellation one pole at −2

answer: Check. The final value is 1/2 = H(0), and the final value theorem agrees: sY(s) = 1/(s + 2) → 1/2 as s → 0, with its pole −2 in the left half-plane. Also dy/dt = e−2t = h(t), as the derivative of a step response must be.

bank.q: A series RC low-pass circuit has input v<sub>in</sub>(t) and output v<sub>C</sub>(t) across the capacitor, with R = 1 kΩ and C = 1 µF. Find H(s), its pole, h(t) and the unit-step response, and give the time constant and the gain at ω = 1000 rad/s.
answer: s-domain circuit. At initial rest the resistor stays R and the capacitor becomes the impedance 1/(sC).
Voltage divider. H(s) = VC(s)/Vin(s) = (1/sC)/(R + 1/sC) = 1/(1 + sRC).

Numbers. RC = (1000 Ω)(1 × 10⁻⁶ F) = 1 × 10⁻³ s = 1 ms. So H(s) = 1/(1 + 0.001s) = 1000/(s + 1000). (Writing 1/(s + 1000) is a common slip: it has the right pole but a d.c. gain of 0.001 instead of 1.)
Pole and stability. One pole at s = −1000 s⁻¹, no finite zero. The circuit is causal with ROC Re(s) > −1000, which contains the jω axis, so it is stable.
Impulse response. h(t) = 1000e−1000tu(t), in s⁻¹ (volts out per volt-second in). Its area is 1000 × (1/1000) = 1 = H(0).
Check of h(t). The initial value theorem gives h(0⁺) = lim sH(s) = lim 1000s/(s + 1000) = 1000 as s → ∞, matching 1000e0 = 1000.

answer.text: Step response. Y(s) = 1000/(s(s + 1000)) = 1/s − 1/(s + 1000), so vC(t) = (1 − e−1000t)u(t) volts for a 1 V step.

answer: Time constant. τ = RC = 1 ms: after one τ the capacitor reaches 63.2% of the step.
Gain at ω = 1000 rad/s. H(j1000) = 1000/(1000 + j1000) = 1/(1 + j), so |H| = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 (−3 dB) and the phase is −45°. This is the cutoff frequency, ωc = 1/RC = 1000 rad/s, about 159 Hz.
Pole-zero plot. One × at σ = −1000 on the negative real axis, no zeros, and the causal ROC Re(s) > −1000 shaded to its right, covering the jω axis.
Low frequencies pass almost unchanged and high frequencies are cut by about ten times per decade: the circuit is a first-order low-pass filter.
Check. vC(∞) = 1 V = H(0), and the final value theorem gives lim sY(s) = 1000/1000 = 1 as s → 0.

bank.q: A system has H(s) = (s + 2)/((s + 1)(s − 1)). List the possible ROCs. For each, find h(t) and say whether the system is causal and whether it is stable. Can this system be both causal and stable?
outline: No ROC gives both; check ∫h = H(0) for the stable case
answer: Poles and zero. Zero at s = −2; poles at s = −1 and s = +1. The poles split the s-plane into three ROCs: Re(s) > 1, −1 < Re(s) < 1 and Re(s) < −1.
Rules. A causal system has an ROC to the right of the rightmost pole. A stable system has an ROC that contains the jω axis, Re(s) = 0.

head: ROC
h(t)
Causal?
Stable?
rows: no: e<sup>t</sup> grows; the ROC misses the jω axis
yes: both terms decay away from t = 0; the ROC contains the jω axis

answer: How each h(t) was found. For a term whose pole lies to the left of the ROC, use 1/(s − p) ↔ eptu(t); for a pole to the right of the ROC, use 1/(s − p) ↔ −eptu(−t). In the strip, the pole −1 is to the left (right-sided term) and the pole +1 is to the right (left-sided term).
Stable case in numbers. ∫|h(t)|dt = ½∫₀∞e−tdt + (3/2)∫−∞0etdt = ½ + 3/2 = 2, finite, as BIBO stability needs.

Shapes of h(t). In the causal case h(t) starts at −½ + 3/2 = 1 at t = 0⁺ and then grows like (3/2)et. In the strip case h(t) is −½e−t for t > 0 and −(3/2)et for t < 0: two tails that both die away from t = 0. In the anti-causal case h(t) is zero for t > 0 and blows up as t → −∞.

Frequency response in the stable case. Only the strip contains the jω axis, so only this system has a frequency response: H(jω) = (jω + 2)/((jω + 1)(jω − 1)) = −(2 + jω)/(1 + ω²). At ω = 0 this is −2, which matches H(0).
Values in the stable case. h(1) = −½e−1 ≈ −0.184 and h(−1) = −(3/2)e−1 ≈ −0.552. The response to an impulse at t = 0 starts before t = 0, which is what non-causal means.
Can a non-causal stable system be used? Not in real time, because the output would need future inputs. It can be used offline, on a recorded signal, where the whole input is known in advance.
Check. In the strip s = 0 is inside the ROC, so ∫h(t)dt must equal H(0) = 2/((1)(−1)) = −2. From the table, ∫h dt = −½·1 − (3/2)·1 = −2. ✓

Conclusion. Causality needs Re(s) > 1, stability needs an ROC containing Re(s) = 0. No ROC does both, because the pole at s = +1 lies in the right half-plane. This system can be causal or stable, but not both.

bank.q: Compare the Fourier transform and the Laplace transform for signal and system analysis. When does the Laplace transform reduce to the Fourier transform? Evaluate which tool suits each of these tasks: a growing signal, the response of a circuit switched on with stored energy, and the steady-state gain of a filter.
outline: Definitions; X(jω) = X(s) at s = jω when the ROC contains the jω axis
Laplace converges for more signals because of e<sup>−σt</sup>
Table of signals: e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t), e<sup>2t</sup>u(t), u(t), cos(ω₀t)
Systems: H(s) gives transient, stability and initial conditions; H(jω) gives steady-state gain and phase
Verdict for each task, with a number
answer: Definitions. Fourier: X(jω) = ∫−∞∞x(t)e−jωtdt. Laplace: X(s) = ∫−∞∞x(t)e−stdt with s = σ + jω. The Laplace transform is the Fourier transform of x(t)e−σt.

When they coincide. Putting σ = 0 gives s = jω. If the ROC of X(s) contains the jω axis, the Fourier transform exists and X(jω) = X(s) at s = jω. If the ROC does not contain the axis, the two are not related by this substitution.

head: Signal
Laplace
Fourier
rows: 1/(jω + 2): exists, the ROC contains the axis
does not exist: the signal grows
only with an impulse: πδ(ω) + 1/(jω), the axis is the ROC boundary
no bilateral transform: the ROC is empty

answer: For systems. H(s) holds the poles, so it shows causality and stability (through the ROC), the transient modes, and, with the one-sided transform, the effect of initial conditions. H(jω) is the frequency response: the gain |H(jω)| and phase ∠H(jω) that a sinusoid meets in the steady state. H(jω) exists only for a stable system.
Task 1, a growing signal such as e2tu(t). Only the Laplace transform works: 1/(s − 2) with ROC Re(s) > 2. Fourier analysis has nothing to offer.

Task 2, a circuit switched on with stored energy. Use the one-sided Laplace transform. For dy/dt + 3y = 2u(t) with y(0⁻) = 1, the initial value enters as −y(0⁻) in sY − 1 + 3Y = 2/s, and y(t) = 2/3 + (1/3)e−3t follows by partial fractions. The Fourier transform has no place for y(0⁻) and describes only the steady state.

Task 3, the steady-state gain of a stable filter. Both work, and the Fourier view is the natural one. For H(s) = 1/(s + 2) at ω = 2 rad/s: H(j2) = 1/(2 + j2), so |H| = 1/√8 ≈ 0.354 and the phase is −45°. The Laplace route gives the same number by putting s = j2, because the ROC Re(s) > −2 contains the axis.

Evaluation. The Laplace transform is the wider tool: it handles growing signals, transients, initial conditions and stability, and contains the Fourier transform as the special case σ = 0. The Fourier transform is the better tool for spectra and steady-state sinusoidal analysis of stable systems, and it also covers two-sided power signals such as cos(ω₀t), which have no bilateral Laplace transform.

The damping factor at work. x(t) = e2tu(t) has no Fourier transform. Multiply by e−σt with σ = 3: e−tu(t) has the Fourier transform 1/(1 + jω). The Laplace transform X(s) = 1/(s − 2) at s = 3 + jω gives 1/(1 + jω), the same thing. So X(s) on any vertical line inside the ROC is the Fourier transform of the damped signal.

On the boundary. cos(2t)u(t) has X(s) = s/(s² + 4) with ROC Re(s) > 0, whose edge is the jω axis itself. Its Fourier transform exists only with impulses at ω = ±2, so s = jω cannot be substituted directly.

head: Task
Tool
Reason
rows: circuit switched on with stored energy
initial conditions enter through sY − y(0⁻)
steady-state gain of a stable filter

bank.q: A causal second-order system has H(s) = ωₙ²/(s² + 2ζωₙs + ωₙ²) with ωₙ = 2 rad/s. Draw the pole locations for ζ = 1.25, 1, 0.5 and 0, find the unit-step response in each case, and explain how the shape of the response and the stability follow from the poles.
outline: ζ = 0: ±j2, sustained oscillation, not BIBO stable
Shape from the real part (decay) and the imaginary part (ringing)
answer: Poles. The roots of s² + 2ζωₙs + ωₙ² = 0 are s = −ζωₙ ± ωₙ√(ζ² − 1). For ζ < 1 they are complex: s = −ζωₙ ± jωd with ωd = ωₙ√(1 − ζ²). With ωₙ = 2, ωₙ² = 4.

svg.aria: Four s-planes with the poles of the second-order system for damping ratio 1.25, 1, 0.5 and 0, with natural frequency 2 rad/s.

answer: ζ = 0.5. Y(s) = 4/(s((s + 1)² + 3)). With A = 1 at s = 0, the rest is −(s + 2)/((s + 1)² + 3) = −[(s + 1) + (1/√3)·√3]/((s + 1)² + (√3)²). So y(t) = 1 − e−t[cos(√3t) + (1/√3)sin(√3t)], with ωd = √3 ≈ 1.732 rad/s. Peak overshoot = e−ζπ/√(1−ζ²) = e−1.814 ≈ 0.163, that is 16.3%, at tp = π/ωd ≈ 1.81 s; the 2% settling time is about 4/(ζωₙ) = 4 s.
ζ = 0. Y(s) = 4/(s(s² + 4)) = 1/s − s/(s² + 4), so y(t) = 1 − cos(2t). It swings between 0 and 2 for ever.

Shape from the poles. The real part −ζωₙ sets the decay: the further left, the faster the transient dies. The imaginary part ωd sets the ringing frequency. Two real poles (ζ > 1) give a slow, non-oscillating rise dominated by the pole nearer the origin (−1). A double pole (ζ = 1) gives the fastest rise without overshoot. A complex pair (0 < ζ < 1) gives overshoot and decaying ringing.

Stability. For ζ > 0 every pole has a negative real part, so the causal system is stable and y(t) → 1 = H(0). For ζ = 0 the poles ±j2 sit on the jω axis: the system is marginal, not BIBO stable. A bounded input at ω = 2 rad/s, such as cos(2t)u(t), produces a response that grows like t sin(2t).

Design reading. For a fast response with no overshoot choose ζ = 1; for a faster rise accept some overshoot with ζ ≈ 0.5 to 0.7; never let ζ reach 0, where the system rings for ever. The table shows the trade: ζ = 0.5 rises in 0.82 s but overshoots by 16.3%, while ζ = 1 takes 1.68 s and does not overshoot.
Check. In every stable case y(0) = 0: 1 − 4/3 + 1/3 = 0; 1 − 1 − 0 = 0; 1 − 1·(1 + 0) = 0. And the final value theorem gives sY(s) = 4/(s² + 2ζωₙs + 4) → 1 as s → 0.

glossary.def: The operation X(s) = ∫x(t)e<sup>−st</sup>dt that maps a time signal to a function of the complex frequency s = σ + jω.
The Laplace transform with the integral over all time, −∞ to ∞; needed for signals that are nonzero for t < 0.
The Laplace transform with the integral from 0⁻ to ∞; it brings initial conditions into differential equations.
The set of s for which the Laplace integral converges; a vertical strip in the s-plane that contains no pole.
The complex plane of s = σ + jω, with σ across and jω up, on which poles, zeros and the ROC are drawn.
A value of s at which X(s) or H(s) becomes infinite: a root of the denominator.
A value of s at which X(s) or H(s) equals zero: a root of the numerator.
A signal that is zero before some time; its ROC lies to the right of its rightmost pole.
A signal that is zero after some time; its ROC lies to the left of its leftmost pole.
A signal that extends to both t → −∞ and t → ∞; its ROC is a strip between two poles, if it exists at all.
A ratio of polynomials whose numerator degree is less than its denominator degree.
Rewriting a proper rational X(s) as a sum of simple terms, each matching a table pair.
The coefficient A of a term A/(s + p) for a simple pole; found by the cover-up rule.
x(0⁺) = lim sX(s) as s → ∞, valid when X(s) is strictly proper.
x(∞) = lim sX(s) as s → 0, valid only when every pole of sX(s) is in the left half-plane.
H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) for an LTI system at initial rest; the Laplace transform of the impulse response.
A system whose impulse response is zero for t < 0; for rational H(s) its ROC is to the right of the rightmost pole.
Every bounded input gives a bounded output; for an LTI system, ∫|h(t)|dt is finite and the ROC of H(s) contains the jω axis.
A causal system with simple poles on the jω axis and none to the right; its modes neither grow nor decay, but it is not BIBO stable.
The part of the output caused by the initial conditions alone, with the input set to zero.
The part of the output caused by the input alone, with all initial conditions zero: Y(s) = H(s)X(s).
H(jω), the transfer function on the jω axis; it exists when the ROC contains the axis and gives gain and phase.
ζ in s² + 2ζωₙs + ωₙ²; ζ > 1 overdamped, ζ = 1 critically damped, 0 < ζ < 1 underdamped, ζ = 0 undamped.
Stability of every mode inside a system, including modes hidden by a pole-zero cancellation in H(s).
